newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army sergeant sentenced to 25 years for rape.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army sergeant sentenced to 25 years for rape.

text.p: Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, a key figure in one of the worst U.S. military sex scandals, was sentenced on Tuesday to 25 years in prison for raping six women and other sexual offences.
Flanked by his three attorneys, Simpson, 32, showed no emotion when the panel returned its finding. He kissed his mother and left the courtroom silently arm in arm with his sister.
The panel also reduced his rank to E-1, the lowest in the Army, forfeiture of pay, and dishonourable discharge. Simpson, a 13-year veteran, will serve his prison term at Ft. Leavenworth, Kansas.
Simpson was the first of 12 trainers charged with various acts of sexual misconduct at the Aberdeen Proving Ground military base to go before a court-martial. He was charged with the most rapes.
He will be eligible for a clemency hearing in five years and for parole after serving eight years and four months. He has already served 238 days of the sentence.
His case, however, is automatically appealed to the Army Court of Criminal Appeals in Falls Church, Virginia, because the sentence exceeds one year in prison.
Lt. Col. Gabriel Riesco, Chief of Staff of the Ordnance Centre and School, said the panel's findings confirmed Simpson used his access and power to manipulate his subordinates.
The Army said it regrets failing to detect the conduct sooner and was working to ensure these crimes were not repeated.
"This should be a flare in the night ... those drill sergeants and instructors who are out there trolling instead of training should think twice," Lt. Col. Riesco said.
But defence attorney Frank Spinner maintained Simpson did not rape anyone and sex was consensual. Spinner also claimed there was undue command influence on the case.
"My position is that the verdict and sentence may be in on Sgt. Simpson. But the verdict is not in on what has happened here in Aberdeen," Spinner said.
"If you are black, if you are an African-American drill sergeant in the Army, you are an endangered species," he said.
In Washington, Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon denied the suggestion of racism, saying the jury had decided a case "of sexual misconduct."
"It has nothing to do with race ... this is an issue of not following the rules," Bacon said of the Army's prosecution of Simpson and other drill sergeants and trainers.
Government attorneys have maintained Simpson used power, rank and even physical force to assault the women.
Prosecutor Capt. Dave Thomas sought the maximum sentence of life in prison, forfeiture of pay, dishonourable discharge and reduction of rank.

He said Simpson went about his crimes methodically. "He's a predator, a sexual predator just like an animal," Thomas said. "He scans the herd, he finds the weakest one and when he gets them alone, he jumps on them."
The case is not only about abuse of power but dishonour, Thomas said. "I challenge you to think of a crime or criminal who is more disgraceful or done more harm to the Army than this man," he added.
Defence attorney Ed Brady, however, asked that Simpson be punitively discharged from the U.S. Army but that he not be incarcerated.

"There isn't any denying the fact that somewhere along the way he got lost, very, very lost," Brady said. "But calling somebody evil and asking you to send them to jail for the rest of his life is another thing entirely."
Brady said Simpson had already been punished because he lost his military career and any future chance of a civilian career because of the conviction.
Simpson last week was found guilty of 18 counts of rape involving six women trainees.

He was acquitted of one additional rape count, but found guilty of indecent assault. He also was found guilty of 25 of 35 other sexual misconduct counts against him, not guilty of seven and guilty of lesser offences on three.
